title: Why You Should Never Show Annoyance At Misbehavior misbehavior/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that visible annoyance at misbehavior hands control of the classroom to students, since it signals that the teacher's peace depends on their behavior. He describes teachers trapped in a cycle of walking on eggshells and avoiding accountability once this dynamic is established. The remedy he offers is to care deeply about students while remaining dispassionate about their choices, relying entirely on a pre-set classroom management plan to absorb the emotional weight of enforcing consequences. He insists this detachment must be genuine, not performed, or the underlying tension will leak through anyway.
points: Reacting emotionally to misbehavior shifts control to the student and signals that the teacher's mood depends on their choices.
Teachers who take misbehavior personally tend to avoid dealing with it, accepting less than they know is best for students.
The goal is to care deeply about students while being genuinely indifferent to whether they choose to misbehave.
A classroom management plan should absorb all the emotional burden of consequences, letting the teacher respond calmly and automatically.
The approach only works if the calm is real; forced composure lets internal frustration surface anyway.
quotes: If you’re struggling with classroom management, then chances are you become annoyed when your students misbehave.
But every time you react emotionally to misbehavior, you shift control over to your students. You step out of the driver’s seat and hand them the keys.
The truth is, to have the well-behaved class you really want, you must maintain your deep care and concern for your students . . . while at the same time not give a whit if they misbehave.
It only works if it’s real. It only works if you truly feel it. If you have to force yourself to keep calm, the internal strife will inevitably bubble to the surface.
The secret is to rely exclusively on your classroom management plan. Let it do its intended job.
